messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Re: package ‘seewave’ is not available (for R version 3.1.1)
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Re: package ‘seewave’ is not available (for R version 3.1.1)
messages.body_plain:
Hi. I just got the same problem to install Seewave on OSX 10.9 (Mavericks). I will give an alternative solution since I had XCode5 installed and I still wasn't able to install Seewave.

Here are the errors I got:

> stft.c:3:11: fatal error: 'sndfile.h' file not found
> stft.c:14:11: fatal error: 'fftw3.h' file not found
> ERROR: compilation failed for package ‘seewave’

As I see there are only 2 libraries missing when trying to compile Seewave on OSX 10.9: sndfile.h and fftw3.h. To get these libraries, the easiest way is:

1. Install Homebrew: http://brew.sh/
2. from OSX Terminal run:
>
> brew install libsndfile
>
> brew install fftw

Once you have these libraries (you can check that you have them in /usr/local/include), you should be able to install Seewave as indicated on the homepage:

3. From the R console type:

> install.packages("seewave", repos="http://cran.at.r-project.org/")

And that's it:
Welcome to seewave!

--
Juan

messages.subject: timer plots question
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using the function timer to locate the start and end of signals. It seems to work perfect but when I plot the start and end of signals as vertical lines on a new oscillogram or spectrogram there is some mismatch between the lines and the start and end of the signals, usually in the signals at the end of the sound file. I think the oscillogram and spectrogram should look similar to the envelope plot from timer, but it does not.

this is an example. The file can be downloaded here: (https://www.dropbox.com/s/9m1gtn2nuznmsau/exampleLBH.wav?dl=0)

w1<-readWave("exampleLBH.wav")

w2<-ffilter(w1, f=f, from = 2000, to = 9000, bandpass = T,wl=300, output="Wave")

#the plot produced by timer looks fine
x<-timer(wave = w2,f =f ,threshold=11, envt="hil", msmooth=c(900,0),
      power=1)

#however there is some part of the signals (mostly the last 2) that is out of the start-end time returned by timer in both
# the oscillogram and spectrogram
oscillo(w1,f=f)
abline(v=c(x$s.start,x$s+x$s.start),col="red",lty="dashed")

spectro(w1,f=f,wl=300,flim=c(1,12),palette = rev.gray.colors.1,scale = F,grid = F,collevels = seq(-50,0,1))
abline(v=c(x$s.start,x$s+x$s.start),col="red",lty="dashed")

I would appreciate any help on this

thank you!

Marcelo

messages.subject: Re: timer plots question
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The issue seems to come from the smoothing parameter used in timer().

Smoothing with a non overlapping window of 900 points induces a downsampling of the original wave and therefore a potential innacurracy in the time measurements. A way to solve this is to use overlapping windows. For instance, a 50% overlap seems to give much better results:

x<-timer(wave = w2,f =f ,threshold=11, envt="hil", msmooth=c(900,50), power=1)

You can also try the ssmooth argument that does not process any downsampling:

x<-timer(wave = w2,f =f ,threshold=11, envt="hil", ssmooth=900, power=1)

HTH

Jerome

messages.subject: fpeaks for a 2D-spectrogram instead of a spec or meanspec?
messages.subject_clean: fpeaks for a 2D-spectrogram instead of a spec or meanspec?
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to obtain the frequency/amp peaks over time in a wav file. If I use fpeaks() on a spec or meanspec, I get a histogram of frequency and amplitude. Instead what I want is a plot (and list) of the peak frequencies over time (ideally limited to some number/second but I can deal with whatever). So, time on the X, freq on the Y, and choose which ones to plot based on peak amplitude of the frequencies.

The spectro() function gives me a plot that is almost what I'm looking for. It plots freq over time and uses color intensity to represent amplitude values. I basically want a plot of that same information, but just a curve of the highest amplitude points.

Is this possible with seewave?

One way to do this would be to use the "amp" matrix which is part of the return value from spectro(), and then manually put together a plot which is to your liking.

Best wishes,
Jesse Ross
